t: Divide Array in Sets of K Consecutive Numbers
o: We must partition all elements of `nums` into groups of exactly `k` distinct consecutive integers (e.g. `x, x+1, ..., x+k-1`). Every element must be used exactly once, and no group may be smaller than `k`. In Example 1 (`k=4`), the groups `[1,2,3,4]` and `[3,4,5,6]` consume all eight numbers. In Example 2, four triples cover everything. In Example 3, with `n=4` not divisible by `k=3`, it is impossible immediately. Constraints allow $O(n \log n)$: sorting or a heap over counts works comfortably for $n \le 10^5$.
k: If n % k != 0 the answer is instantly false.
Greedily start each set at the smallest remaining value; this never hurts because that smallest value can only belong to a set starting at itself.
A count map plus processing values in sorted order lets us 'consume' runs of k consecutive numbers in near-linear time.

a.i: Keep a min-heap of the distinct values still present, with a count map. Repeatedly take the smallest available value x and try to remove one copy each of x..x+k-1. If any of them is missing, return false. This directly simulates building sets from the smallest leftover number, which is always safe since nothing smaller remains to pair with it.
s: Build a count map and push all distinct keys into a min-heap.
While the heap is non-empty, peek the smallest value x.
For i in [x, x+k): if count[i] == 0 return false; decrement count[i].
After consuming, pop exhausted values from the heap top; when done, return true.
a.t: O(n log n) — each element is consumed once, and heap/map operations cost logarithmic time.
a.sp: O(n) — for the count map and heap of distinct values.

a.i: Sort the array and sweep left to right. For each value x that still has an unassigned count c > 0, we are forced to open c sets starting at x, so we subtract c from the counts of x+1 ... x+k-1. If any of those drops negative, no valid partition exists. This avoids re-scanning consumed elements and needs only a sort plus one linear pass.
s: Sort nums and build a count map.
Iterate over sorted values; skip values whose remaining count is zero.
Let c be the remaining count of x; subtract c from counts of x+1 .. x+k-1; if any goes below zero, return false.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the greedy pass touches each element O(k) times but total decrements are bounded by n*k spread across groups, effectively O(n log n).
a.sp: O(n) — for the hash map of counts.

w: In an interview, lead with the divisibility check, then present the greedy 'start at the smallest value' argument — it is the crux of correctness. The sorted-count approach is the cleanest optimal solution; the heap version is equivalent but slightly heavier. Pitfalls: forgetting the `n % k` check, allowing duplicate values inside one set (each set uses *distinct* consecutive integers), and off-by-one errors on the range `x .. x+k-1`. Edge cases: `k = 1` (always true), all-equal arrays with `k > 1` (false), and large value ranges where a bucket-array approach would blow memory — hence a hash map. Follow-ups often ask for the same solution applied to LeetCode 846 (identical problem) or returning the actual groups instead of a boolean.
